Introduction 43 The need for guidance on pharmacovigilance specifically for the use of medicinal products in pregnancy 44 is widely recognised. The use of medicinal products during breastfeeding is also an area in need of 45 further pharmacovigilance guidance. This is because, in addition to the benefits and risks of 55 the medicine for the woman, the potential risks to the (unborn) child also need to be taken into 56 account. candidates.statement: Because pregnant women are rarely included in clinical trials, at the time of marketing authorisation, 107 assessment of potential risks associated with the use of medicinal products in pregnancy usually relies 108 on the extrapolation from non-clinical data and on knowledge of adverse embryo/foetal reactions of 109 other products with similar pharmacological properties. There are many examples where the 110 mechanism of action of the medicine is related to the mechanism of teratogenicity or adverse 111 embryo/foetal reaction, and hence pharmacological-toxicological class effects have been observed. 112 Consequently, when assessing potential risks for an active substance, known adverse pregnancy 113 outcomes for another substance of the same class of medicinal products should be carefully 114 considered. However, evidence of absence of harm to the child for one substance cannot be 115 extrapolated to other substances of the same class and be interpreted as indicating the absence of a 116 potential risk for these other substances. Exposure through semen is another route of exposure to the 117 embryo or foetus. Whether this carries a risk in clinical practice is unknown at present, but this should 118 be considered for highly teratogenic substances that are transmitted into semen. 119 Like pregnant women, breastfeeding women are usually excluded from clinical trials; therefore the 120 estimation of risks for breastfed infants at the time of marketing authorisation may be based on 121 pharmacokinetic (PK) data, on data about the severity of potential adverse reactions to the medicine in 122

Some adverse pregnancy outcomes only become apparent 165 long after exposure has occurred, as the child develops, irrespective of when the exposure occurred. 166 Adverse pregnancy outcomes can therefore not be evaluated in isolation, and this needs to be 167 accounted for in any evaluation or study design. 168 Overall, birth defects that are visible at birth are relatively frequent at around ~3% of all live births; 169 however, the frequency of each individual birth defect is considerably lower (and has been reported as 170 ranging from 1 in 700 to 1 in 30 000 live births, or less). If a product is harmful in utero , it is unlikely 171 to cause a detectable increase in the frequency of all birth defects. Instead, the frequency of some 172 specific, but not all birth defects, may increase. Typically, in the population of pregnant women there 173 are limited numbers of exposure to a medicine; therefore, there will be an even smaller number of 174 adverse pregnancy outcomes (i.e. ‘adverse events of special interest’ for data collection and analysis). 175 This has implications for the numbers of spontaneously reported adverse events and on cases 176 identified through post-authorisation surveillance methods, as numbers are expected to be small, 177 making it difficult to identify an increase in cases of a rare adverse reactions. It also means ‘birth 178 defects’ in general should not be studied as one single outcome (P.III.B.4.). 179 P.III.A.1.4. Adverse events in the child following exposure through 180 breastfeeding 181
